variants.name: Recursive generic constraint (CRTP in C#)
variants.idiom_name: abstract class Base<T> where T : Base<T> with a T-returning accessor
variants.implementation_notes: C# has no templates and no non-virtual dispatch over a class hierarchy, but a recursive generic constraint reproduces CRTP's structure: abstract class Builder<T> where T : Builder<T> plus an accessor that returns the concrete type gives fluent builders and self-typed APIs, and the official docs use the same shape (IDescribable<T> where T : IDescribable<T>). Because the CLR still dispatches instance members virtually and the (T)this conversion is checked at runtime rather than proven, the idiom buys compile-time self-typing and one shared base implementation, not vtable-free calls; use it when derived types must appear in signatures and return types.
pitfalls: The constraint does not prove identity: class Apple : Builder<Orange> compiles whenever Orange : Builder<Orange>, and the (T)this conversion then throws InvalidCastException at runtime - C# cannot express 'T is exactly this class'.
The CLR dispatches instance members virtually regardless of the recursive bound, so the C# form gains type safety, not speed; do not present it as a performance pattern.
Each constructed generic type gets its own static storage, which makes per-type counters work, but a shared non-generic registry must be added explicitly when all types must be counted together.

variants.name: Static abstract/virtual interface members (C# 11)
variants.idiom_name: static abstract interface member invoked through a type parameter
variants.implementation_notes: C# 11 lets an interface declare static abstract / static virtual members that implementing types supply and that are resolved by the compiler through the type parameter: the language reference states these members 'don't have a runtime dispatch mechanism analogous to virtual or abstract methods'. That removes the need for self-referential recursion when the base has to invoke per-implementing-type code - System.Numerics.INumber<TSelf> and the generic math interfaces are the flagship use - while a self-referential constraint such as where T : IDescribable<T> remains the way to name the implementing type in signatures.
pitfalls: Static abstract members can be called only through a type parameter, never on an interface value (CS8926), so code holding an instance must be reshaped as a generic method.

If any static abstract member lacks a most specific implementation in the interface, the interface cannot be used as a type argument (CS8920); default implementations must cover what algorithms do not supply.
Operators declared in interfaces have placement rules (one operand must be the containing type or its constrained type parameter), so the mixin surface is narrower than CRTP's friend operators.
